The Croatian DPA reprimanded a bank for publishing the personal data of prize game winners on its web page contrary to the principles of lawfulness and fairness of Article 5 GDPR and without a legal basis under Article 6 GDPR.

Following several complaints, the CNIL carried out an online inspection of two websites run by the Google group and found that users could not refuse cookies as simply as they could accept them. The restricted committee found a breach of Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act (the ePrivacy cookie rule) by both companies. It fined Google LLC (the US company) EUR 90 million and Google Ireland Limited (the Irish company) EUR 60 million, EUR 150 million in total. The published decision masks both companies' names; the CNIL's own press release names them. It also ordered both to change how consent is collected from users in France, with a daily penalty of EUR 100,000 after three months, and ordered the decision to be published. The committee noted the very large number of people concerned, the profits drawn from advertising, and that the companies had been recently sanctioned for related cookie failings.

The French DPA fined Facebook Ireland Limited €60,000,000 for failing to comply with Article 82 of the Loi 'Informatique et Libertés', and ordered the company to modify the website "facebook.com" to offer French users a means of refusing to give consent that is as simple as the mechanism provided for their acceptance.

The Greek DPA examined two complaints about promotional telephone calls (one live-agent call and one automated call) telling recipients they had won a prize, with a premium-rate number to call back for 'discount gift vouchers'. The calls came from numbers held by PLUS REAL ADVERTISMENT, which claimed participants had consented by entering their details in its promotions. The Authority found infringements of Articles 13 and 14 GDPR and of Article 11 of Law 3471/2006 (unsolicited communications), noting the controller aimed at financial gain, had no complaint-handling procedure and did not obtain valid consents. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 25,000.

Over several years the Authority received ten complaints about automated promotional calls (and one SMS) offering prizes or supermarket vouchers, without identifying the company on whose behalf they were made. The numbers were traced to INCOSER, which claimed participants had signed up themselves and consented. The Authority found breaches of the information duties in Articles 13 and 14 GDPR and of Article 11 of Law 3471/2006 (unsolicited calls, including to numbers on the opt-out register). It imposed a fine of EUR 30,000, noting the company profited financially, had no complaints procedure, did not respond in time to the Authority and was ignorant of the legal framework, but is now inactive.

The Croatian DPA rejected a data subject’s complaint against a newspaper, claiming it did not have a legal basis to publish their personal data. The DPA held that the processing was necessary for the public interest and that there was no violation of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR.

The CNIL investigated a furniture retailer selling online and in store in several EU countries. It found that the company had no retention periods for customer and prospect data and kept data for excessive periods, gave incomplete information to individuals, and had breaches concerning erasure requests, processor contracts and security. The CNIL initially planned only an order, but the Berlin authority raised a relevant and reasoned objection asking for a fine. The Restricted Committee found the breaches of Articles 5(1)(e), 13, 17, 28 and 32 GDPR established and imposed a fine of EUR 120,000. It imposed no injunction because the company had brought itself into compliance during the proceedings.

A citizen trying to log in to the Ministry of Tourism's 'Tourism for All' platform with tax credentials was shown another person's application data, including tax and social security numbers, contact details and disability fields. The Ministry did not notify the breach to the Authority, and its listed DPO email address was inactive because no DPO had been designated at the time. The Authority found breaches of Articles 13, 32, 33 and 37 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 75,000 on the Ministry.

The French DPA fined the payment service provider SLIMPAY €180,000 for failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, and to report a data breach which affected over 12,000,000 data subjects.

The French DPA (CNIL) fined a mobile operator €300,000 for failing to respect customers' right of access and right to object by not responding to their access requests in a timely manner and sending them marketing messages despite having been notified of their objection to such processing.
The Finnish DPA imposed a fine of €5,000 on a medical clinic for not implementing the data subject's access request and failing to inform data subjects about the processing of personal data.
The Austrian DPA held that the use of Google Analytics by an Austrian website provider led to transfers of personal data to Google LLC in the U.S. in violation of Chapter V. of the GDPR.

The Danish DPA (Datatilsynet) criticised the (Danish) Conservative People's Party for sending letters to potential voters without giving information about how their names and addresses had been obtained, in violation of Article 14 GDPR.

The Portuguese DPA issued a €1,250,000 fine against the Lisbon Municipality for sharing personal and sensitive data of protestors with third parties, including the embassies and foreign ministers of the countries targeted by the protests.

The DPA held that neither EU law or national law require that the controller replies to an access request containing "criminal data" or “sensitive data” delivering the information by hand. An answer can be given by electronic means, especially if the data subject asked so.
The Italian DPA imposed multiple corrective measures and a fine of €26,513,977 on Enel Energia for unlawfully processing the personal data of millions of users for telemarketing purposes.
The Finnish DPA imposed a fine of €6,500 on a travel agency for failing to adequately secure the personal data and for failing to comply with the data subject's request to erase their personal data.
The DPA imposed a fine of €52,000 on the Finnish Motor Insurers' Centre for processing and requesting unnecessary patient information from healthcare providers.

A preventive medicine centre notified the Garante of a hacker attack in which a group obtained metadata (name, date of birth, type of radiological exam) of five patients from its PACS server and posted a partly obscured image on Twitter. The server was reachable from the internet without authentication, apparently via a router port-forwarding configuration. The Garante found the security measures inadequate and also found that the centre had not published or communicated its data protection officer's contact details. It declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5, 25, 32 and 37 GDPR and fined the centre EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

A former employee complained that his individualised work email accounts stayed active after his employment ended and that his deletion request went unanswered. The Garante found that Corradi s.r.l. was the controller, kept the account active until October 2019 without informing him, and ignored three requests for information from the authority. It found breaches of fairness, minimisation, storage limitation and information duties, plus failure to respond to the Garante. It imposed a EUR 20,000 fine and ordered publication of the decision.

A bank customer complained that a letter from Ubi Banca bore on the outside of the envelope the words 'credito anomalo Chieti' (anomalous credit), which could reveal his financial situation to third parties. The Garante found this breached the principles of lawfulness, fairness and transparency and of data minimisation, contrary to its 2005 debt-recovery guidance. It imposed a fine of EUR 100,000 on the bank (now merged into Intesa Sanpaolo) and ordered publication of the decision. The bank had already replaced the wording with a code during the investigation, and this was treated as mitigating.

A UK customer complained to the UK authority that FCA Italy had not given him access to transcripts of calls with its customer service centre and to the internal case notes about his vehicle problem. The Garante, as lead authority, found that FCA failed to answer the access request within the deadline and did not give adequate reasons for withholding the data. It rejected FCA's arguments on the applicable law and on the right of defence. It declared the processing unlawful, ordered FCA to hand over the complainant's personal data in the case notes within 30 days, and fined it EUR 20,000. The Austrian authority's objection was taken into account in a revised draft decision.

The Belgian Litigation Chamber examined a bank's information systems, notably whether they allowed data subjects to exercise their rights (rectification, diacritical signs in names), after an Inspection Service investigation. It dismissed the findings on Articles 5(1)(d), 16 and 25. It found a violation of Article 38(6) GDPR because the data protection officer held a function creating a conflict of interests (head of a department). It ordered the bank to bring the processing into compliance and imposed a fine of EUR 75,000, reduced from the EUR 100,000 initially envisaged after mitigating circumstances were considered. The Art. 30 complaint was also found not to be a violation.

The UK DPA (ICO) fined an electric utilities company approximately €88,000 (£75,000) for making over 60,000 direct marketing calls to individuals who were registered with the TPS or CTPS and who had not provided valid consent.

The Norwegian DPA imposed a fine of about €20,000 (NOK 200,000) on Elektro & Automasjon Systemer AS for not implementing appropriate technical and organisational measures to prevent unlawful processing, and therefore mistakenly conducting a credit check without legal basis.

The Romanian DPA fined a wholesale pharmacist with approximately €2.000 because it ignored the DPA's request to provide information regarding its processing operations in violation of Article 58(1) GDPR.

The Norwegian DPA investigated Grindr after complaints from the Norwegian Consumer Council. It found that Grindr's earlier consent mechanism was not valid, because consent was not freely given. The free version of the app was conditional on consenting to data sharing with advertising partners, there was no separate consent for different purposes, and refusing meant paying for the premium version. Grindr therefore disclosed users' personal data, including GPS location and special category data, to advertising partners without a legal basis. The DPA found breaches of Articles 6(1) and 9(1) GDPR and imposed an administrative fine of NOK 65,000,000, noting several aggravating factors and one mitigating factor (the new consent mechanism).

A company, EAS, ran a credit check on a private individual who was a part-owner of a competitor, although the person had no customer or other relationship with it. EAS said it was a mistake made while using the Bisnode tool when reviewing a competitor's accounts. The Norwegian DPA found there was no legal basis under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR and fined the company NOK 200,000, reduced from a notified NOK 250,000 because of the company's Covid-related fall in turnover. It also ordered the company to improve its internal controls and procedures for credit checks.
The Irish DPC imposed an administrative fine of €110,000 against a city council due to numerous failings in meeting data protection obligations in some of its smart city initiatives.

The Polish DPA imposed a fine of approximately €9900 (PLN 45,000) on a public university for failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to continuously ensure the confidentiality of processing activities, as well as for failing to regularly test, measure and evaluate the effectiveness of these measures.

The complainant received an unsolicited marketing letter from the defendant, which had bought his data from a third party. He asked by email and registered letter for the source of his data, objected and requested erasure, but got no reply. A first 'light' decision (69/2020) ordered compliance; the defendant again did not respond. In this decision on the merits, the Litigation Chamber found breaches of Articles 12.3, 14, 15, 17.1.c and 21.2 GDPR. It ordered the defendant to give Article 14 information to all people whose data came from the third party and imposed a fine of EUR 10,000. The complainant eventually declared himself satisfied.

Seventeen individuals complained about promotional telephone calls made on behalf of the gas supplier ZENITH by its call-centre processor One Way, to numbers listed in the Article 11 opt-out register. The cause was an employee's omission and the lack of an automated process excluding registered numbers from the call lists, over more than 1.5 million calls in the period. The Authority fined the processor EUR 30,000 for breaching Article 32(2) and (4) GDPR in conjunction with Article 28(3)(c). It reprimanded the controller ZENITH for breaching Article 28(3)(c), because its oversight and instructions were only general and insufficient.

The Finnish DPA fined a psychotherapy firm €608,000 for not reporting two personal data breaches in due time, which led to the disclosure of patient records to the attackers responsible for the breaches, and for failing to ensure the security of personal data. Both the firm and the patients were blackmailed following these data breaches.
CNIL reminds controller that all processing types must be covered within the relevant privacy policy or this may constitute a breach of Article 12 GDPR and Article 13 GDPR.

The Norwegian DPA fined the company Trumf €500,185 (NOK 5,000,000) for failing to report and document repeated data breaches where people could register other people's bank account numbers to get access to their detailed purchase history.

After an investigation concluded in November 2021, the Romanian authority found that Telekom Romania Communications had collected inaccurate personal data, in particular an email address, and so sent invoices and arrears notices about another subscriber to an unrelated person who complained. It also found that the company did not act on an erasure request. Two fines were imposed, RON 24,745 (about EUR 5,000) and RON 4,949 (about EUR 1,000), together with corrective measures on data accuracy, security and handling of erasure and rectification requests.
The UK DPA (ICO) fined Virgin Media limited GBP 50,000 for sending direct marketing emails in violation of Regulation 22 PECR.

A local health authority in Parma mistakenly put two patients' diagnostic reports into an envelope addressed to a third patient and sent it by registered mail, while the third patient's own report was not enclosed. The third patient complained and the authority also notified a data breach. The Garante found the disclosure of health data unlawful, in breach of Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR. It fined the authority EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision, but imposed no corrective orders because the authority had already adopted measures.

A complaint revealed that the online traffic-fine payment portal run by Ica s.r.l. for the Municipality of Collegno let anyone view other people's fine data by entering only a predictable report number and date, because the licence-plate requirement was lost in a software update. The Garante found that Ica, as processor, had not applied adequate security measures, breaching Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR. The pedestrian-fine aspect was treated as resolved since no personal data were involved. It imposed a fine of EUR 30,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

The Data Protection Commission conducted an own-volition inquiry into the Teaching Council after personal data breaches involving unauthorised access to two staff email accounts. It found the Council infringed Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) by failing to apply appropriate security, and Article 33(1) by not notifying the breach without undue delay. The Council was treated as a public body, so the fine cap was EUR 1,000,000. It was fined EUR 40,000 for the security infringement and EUR 20,000 for the notification infringement, EUR 60,000 in total, and an order to bring processing into compliance and a reprimand were also imposed.

A nursing home notified a data breach after the hacker group LulzSec_ITA published radiology images on Twitter. The hackers had accessed the remote image viewer MedDream, supplied and installed by Med Store Saronno (the nursing home's processor), using default admin/admin credentials over unencrypted http. The Garante found that the processor's security measures (insecure network protocol and no password policy) were inadequate, breaching Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1). It imposed a fine of EUR 7,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no corrective measures because the conduct had ceased to have effects.

A private clinic notified the Garante of a breach: a hacker group got into its remote radiology image viewer (MedDream) using the default admin/admin credentials over unencrypted http, and posted radiological images on Twitter. The Garante found the clinic, together with its processor, had not adopted adequate security measures (no encryption in transit, weak password practice). It treated the fault as slight negligence, noting a single isolated incident, prompt remediation and full cooperation. It declared the processing unlawful and fined the clinic EUR 30,000, with publication of the decision.

The CNPD opened an investigation into a transport company's video surveillance and on 20 March 2019 carried out an on-site visit. The restricted formation found that one camera permanently watched the receptionist and another covered a smokers' corner used by staff in their free time. Seven cameras also covered neighbouring land or the public road, which breached data minimisation. The company had also not given adequate information to data subjects under Article 13. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 6,800, which the company had accepted, and ordered no corrective measures because the company had already taken compliance steps.

A complaint was lodged with the Polish DPA against a company over the processing of the complainant's data. The President of UODO asked the company for explanations four times; one letter was received and the other three were treated as delivered after uncollected postal notices, yet the company never replied. The authority opened separate own-initiative proceedings and found breaches of Articles 31 and 58(1)(e) GDPR (lack of cooperation and no access to information). It imposed an administrative fine of PLN 18,192 (about EUR 4,000), treating the failure to provide access to information as the most serious breach under Art. 83(3).

The Greek DPA fined two mobile telecommunications company COSMOTE and its parent company OTE, €6,000,000 and €3,250,000 respectively. The first for failing to carry out the data protection impact assessment under Article 35(7) GDPR, for not complying with the principle of transparency under Article 5(1) GDPR and for not anonymising the data under Article 25(1) GDPR, among others. The second for failing to implement the appropriate technical and organisational measures under Article 32 GDPR.

The Belgian DPA found that a public authority infringed the GDPR by disclosing the identity of a complainant to four suspects in the context of a municipal administrative sanction procedure for illegal dumping. Since the public authority adopted measures to avoid future infringements, the Belgian DPA decided not to impose a fine.

The DPA confirmed that the processing of personal data under the Prevention of Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism Act is legally based on Article 6(1)(c) GDPR, which allows processing necessary for compliance with a legal obligation.

The Lithuanian DPA (VDAI) imposed a fine of €110,000 on UAB Prime Leasing for a lack of organisational and technical measures to ensure security of processing under Article 32(1)(a), Article 32(1)(b), and Article 32(1)(d) GDPR, which led to a data breach.
The UK DPA (ICO) fined EB Associates Group Limited approximately €164,500 (GBP 140,000) for instigating over 107,000 illegal cold calls to individuals about pensions schemes.

The Icelandic DPA ruled that processing of blood samples in connection with Covid-19 research by a genetic company was unlawful because the data subjects were not informed beforehand about the further processing of their personal data for that purpose.

The French DPA (CNIL) ordered Clearview AI, a company conducting facial recognition on public web sources, to stop unlawfully collecting and processing the personal data of data subjects on the French territory, delete all such personal data collected previously, and set up clearer and more efficient procedures that enable the enforcement of the right of access and right to be forgotten.

The Icelandic DPA rejected a data subject's claim that their employer failed to comply with an access request they made, because of a lack of evidence of a breach and the fact that labour law should be applied instead of data protection law.
The Danish DPA reprimands a municipality for not using end-to-end encryption on sensitive content sent by email, and for still using TLS 1.1 in spite of the protocol's well known security flaws.

The Garante's newsletter reports that it fined the company that commissioned an SMS promotional campaign, as controller, for never checking that the marketing company it hired followed the contract instructions. The data came from unverified lists through a chain of subcontractors, some set up abroad without a representative in Italy. Two complainants had kept receiving unwanted messages and received no satisfactory answers. The commissioning company was fined EUR 400,000; a second company, the marketing supplier, was banned from using data from non-compliant sources and fined EUR 200,000; a third was fined EUR 90,000 for not replying to the Garante's requests.

The Dutch DPA fined the Minister of Finance a total of EUR 2,750,000 because the Tax Administration's Benefits department processed nationality data without a lawful basis. It kept the dual nationality of Dutch citizens in its TVS system, used nationality as an indicator in a risk-classification model for childcare benefit applications, and used nationality in detecting organised fraud. The last two processings were also unfair (discriminatory) under Article 5(1)(a). Three separate fines of EUR 750,000, 1,000,000 and 1,000,000 were imposed, with the fairness breaches taken into account in setting the amounts rather than fined separately.

A health services company notified a personal data breach: two medical reports (a blood count and an ECG without trace) of one patient were put by mistake in the envelope of another patient and handed to that person. The company said it was a single human error and pointed to its procedures and quick recovery of the documents. The Garante found the disclosure of health data had no legal basis and breached Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR. It fined the company EUR 6,000, ordered publication of the decision, and adopted no corrective measures because the conduct had ended.

The Norwegian DPA fined the Public Service Pension Fund (SPK) € 99,940 (NOK 1,000,000) for obtaining unnecessary income data of approximately 24,000 people receiving disability pension, in breach of Article 5(1)(c), Article 5(1)(e), Article 6(1), and Article 9(2) GDPR.

Persónuvernd opened an own-initiative inquiry into the government's 'Ferðagjöf' (travel gift) app, built by YAY ehf., after many tips that it demanded extensive personal data and wide access to users' phones. It found that the ministry (ANR), as controller, broke several basic data protection rules and fined it ISK 7,500,000. It found that YAY ehf. failed to ensure adequate security and data protection by design: there was no processing agreement, the app's settings were not properly configured, and the app mistakenly requested broad phone permissions and collected age and gender. YAY ehf. was fined ISK 4,000,000, less ISK 800,000 for the cost of the Syndis security audit. YAY ehf. was not fined for programming the broad access permissions, because the rules were not clear enough to cover steps that did not actually give access. Both parties were ordered to give users proper information before they register.
The Icelandic DPA ordered the Chief Epidemiologist to enter into a new processing agreement with a processor used for SARS-CoV-2 screening and antibody testing.

The Icelandic DPA found that the Ministry of Industries and Innovation and the company YAY contravened the GDPR by collecting personal data without a legal basis and processing it without consent, violated the principle of data minimisation, and failed to comply with its information obligations by processing the personal data of the users of a gift card application, and imposed administrative fines of approximately €50,800 (7,500,000 ISK) and €27,100 (4,000,000 ISK) respectively.

The Icelandic DPA issued a reprimand against a hospital appointed to carry out COVID-19 tests for failing to conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment in violation of Article 35(1) GDPR when relocating part of their staff to another medical centre.

The Hessian DPA (HBDI) held that a data subject has a right to rectification under Article 16 GDPR, even if he or she purposefully provided incorrect information during the account creation in order to circumvent age restrictions.

The Hellenic DPA rejected a complaint by a data subject about possible automated decision-making by a bank on the grounds that there was no new evidence brought forward by the claimant. The DPA also highlighted that the data subject did not exercise their right to object under Article 21(1) GDPR.

The Swedish DPA issued two warnings to the Swedish Migration Agency (the Agency) because it was not clear if the IT-documentation of the Visa Information System (VIS) was adopted by the Agency and because the Agency lacked clear routines for deleting user logs.

The Icelandic DPA dismissed a complaint relating to the publication and sharing of pictures of a teenage child on Facebook, on the ground that it was not competent to rule on whether the parties involved in this publication had exceeded the limits of their freedom of expression.

The Croatian DPA determined that a photograph of a person camouflaged in a jacket and wearing a protective mask did not consitute personal data according to Article 4(1) GDPR because it was impossible for the average person to identify the individual. As a result, the publication did not infringe the GDPR.

The Greek DPA issued a reprimand against the Hellenic Ministry of Education and Religious Affairs for not conducting a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) in an appropriate manner before implementing a method of distance learning after the closure of schools in Greece in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The UK DPA (ICO) imposed a fine of approximately €585,739 (GBP 500,000) on the Cabinet Office for a data breach in violation of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) GDPR. The New Years 2020 Honours List was published including postal addresses for the recipients of the Honours.

Vodafone Romania was sanctioned approx €2,900 for failing to implement sufficient technical and organisational measures which led to the unauthorised access and disclosure of personal data belonging to 70 natural persons.

The Dutch DPA (AP) imposed a fine of €400,000 on Transavia Airlines C.V. for not having taken appropriate technical and organisational measures, which led to a (sensitive) data breach, in violation of Article 32(1) and Article 32(2) GDPR

The Norwegian DPA held that Article 6(1)(b) GDPR «Necessary for the performance of a contract» can not be used as a lawful basis for direct marketing purposes, when direct marketing is not the main subject-matter of the contract in question.

The Belgian DPA considered that it was competent to review the lawfulness of data processing operations which, although having started before 25 May 2018, had continued after that date, but that it was not competent for one-off or multiple processing operations that only took place before then (i.e. before the application date of the GDPR).

The Belgian DPA issued a reprimand against a fitness club for violating Article 5(1)(b) and Article 6 GDPR by sharing the personal data of a member of the club with another member in the context of a payment dispute.

The Luxembourg DPA fined a car dealership €1500 for failing to comply with the principle of data minimisation by not limiting the field of vision of its video surveillance systems as well as inadequately informing both its employees and third parties of their existence.

The Finnish DPA ordered Bisnode Finland Oy to delete incorrect entries from their credit information register and change their procedure of the processing information on debtors’ ability or willingness to pay, because this was in violation of Article 25(1) GDPR.

The Finnish DPA ordered the Legal Register Centre to implement appropriate measures to ensure compliance with the GDPR by ensuring that no incorrect payment information is sent without a legal basis to credit reporting companies.

The Finnish DPA ordered Suomen Asiakastieto Oy to delete incorrect entries from their credit information register and change their procedure of the processing information on debtors’ ability or willingness to pay, because this was in violation of Article 25(1) GDPR.
Danish DPA reprimands a region for using a health care IT system that made it possible for users to access other users' personal data by modifying the URL of the website.

The Catalan DPA issued an opinion stating that access to document requests of administrative proceedings for environmental infringements should not include the personal data of individual polluters, except in cases of “very serious” infringements.
The Danish DPA reprimanded a large consumer goods retailer for failing to implement adequate access control to the personal information of its employees stored on the company's shared drive.

The Icelandic DPA issued an injunction against a private individual to stop monitoring some shared and public areas around a multi-family house through video surveillance cameras, and to delete all the recorded material.

THE ANSPDCP (Romanian DPA) fined IKEA Romania approx €1,000 for a data breach where personal data was erroneously made available online on an IKEA members' platform. The incident affected the personal data of 114 data subjects, half of which were minors.

Romania's data protection authority finished an investigation into the energy producer Hidroelectrica, which began after the company sent several personal data breach notifications. It found that the company lacked adequate technical and organisational security measures, so the personal data of 325 individuals was accessed or disclosed to wrong recipients. It also found that the company kept processing the data of 3 customers after they had asked for erasure and withdrawn consent. The company received a fine of 24,739.50 lei (about EUR 5,000) for the security failure and a warning for the unlawful processing, plus corrective measures to review its security measures, train staff and keep data accurate.

The French DPA (CNIL) imposed a fine of €400,000 on the state-owned public transport operator 'RATP' for collecting and storing data on how many days its agents were on strike in files normally used to determine promotions. The CNIL also found a breach of the principle of storage limitation and data security.

The Finnish DPA found that national legislation on patient data, read together with the GDPR, does not allow the processing of patient data for the professional development of healthcare professionals.

The Finnish DPA ruled that a cleaning company breached the GDPR by using WhatsApp instant messaging services with its employees as a mean to share information about its customers, including their names, address, door code or key box code. Among other things, the controller had no means to oversee the use of personal data via WhatsApp, or otherwise impose restrictions on possible further use.

The Luxembourg DPA (CNPD) found that the offering of a loyalty programme by a company to its customers did not amount to a regular and systematic monitoring of the customers pursuant to Article 37(1)(b) GDPR, and that the Company therefore did not need to appoint a Data Protection Officer.

The Luxembourg DPA found that a non-profit association, which belonged to a confederation of entities providing social services, had wrongfully concluded that it was obliged to appoint a DPO pursuant to Article 37(1) GDPR. However, as no violation had occurred, it closed the case.

As part of a thematic audit campaign on data protection officers, the CNPD investigated a Luxembourg bank. It found that the DPO's contact details were not published, the DPO was not involved formally and regularly in all data protection matters, the DPO's autonomy and reporting line to top management were not formally guaranteed, and the DPO's monitoring task was not shown to be adequately carried out at the start of the investigation. Remedial steps taken during the investigation did not cancel the breaches. The restricted formation imposed a single fine of EUR 18,700 and ordered the company to put a formal mechanism guaranteeing DPO autonomy in place within four months.

The CNPD opened a thematic audit campaign on the data protection officer (DPO) role in 2018, including an audit of a transport company. The investigator found failures to involve the DPO in all data protection issues, to guarantee the DPO's autonomy, and in the DPO's information/advisory and monitoring tasks. The restricted committee upheld breaches of Articles 38(1), 38(3), 39(1)(a) and 39(1)(b) GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 15,400 and ordered the company to comply with Article 39(1)(b) within four months by ensuring the DPO can monitor GDPR compliance.

A customer complained that a car service dealer passed his email and vehicle data to the importer, who sent him unsolicited satisfaction surveys. The authority rejected the complaint against the dealer, but of its own motion found the importer processed the complainant's data without proper individual information or a valid legal basis. It also found the importer's general customer-satisfaction survey practice unlawful (transparency, data minimisation, legal basis, information). It fined the importer HUF 5,000,000 and ordered it to bring processing into compliance within 30 days.

Hungarian DPA fines car importer €13,500 (HUF 5,000,000) for sending client satisfaction surveys without a lawful legal ground, and breaching the principles of transparency, accountability and data minimisation in the process.

The ICO issued a penalty of £36,000 against Unite the Union for unsolicited direct marketing calls (in violation of Regulation 21 PECR) to 57,665 individuals who had not given informed valid consent to receive such calls.

The Belgian DPA dismissed a complaint regarding unsecured contact forms on a hospital website because the complainant had not fill any of these forms, but was pursuing a general public concern without having a personal stake in the case.
The Spanish DPA fined a controller €20,000 (reduced to €16,000) for implementing a biometric identification system without carrying out a DPIA beforehand.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation at Glove Technology SRL on 23.09.2021. It found that the company monitored employees with audio-video cameras in offices without proving a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR, and so breached the lawfulness principle of Article 5(1)(a). It fined the company 24,745 lei (about EUR 5,000) and ordered it to bring the processing into compliance, stop the audio-video processing and delete the related data records. The investigation began after a complaint about cameras recording employees and their conversations.
The Spanish DPA fined a bank €3,000,000 for carrying out profiling for marketing purposes without obtaining valid consent, since it was not specific nor informed.

The Finnish DPA held that a controller, upon receiving an access request from a data subject, was not obliged to provide a copy of a phone call between them in audio format, but could instead provide a written transcript of the call as long as its contents were not edited.

The Danish DPA ruled that a company had failed to obtain the valid consent of data subjects for the placing of cookies because the pop-up cookie banner on the website was designed to make it more difficult to reject the use of cookies than to accept such use.

The State Labor Court of Baden-Württemberg held that in the letter of invitation to BEM, the names of the parties to whom health data will be disclosed must be explicitly listed and the data subject must be informed of the consent and its necessity.

The Danish DPA reprimanded a high school for not reporting a data breach, in violation of Article 33 GDPR. The breach was caused by a human error and consisted in the sending of a warning message to the wrong student with respect to the absence rate of another student.

The Norwegian DPA fined a municipality €409,768 (NOK 4,000,000) for breaches of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, Article 24 GDPR and Article 32 GDPR after a serious ransomware attack led to highly sensitive personal data being irreparably lost and sold on the dark web.

The Spanish DPA fined Vodafone €80,000 (reduced to €64,000) for allowing a third party to enter a contract with the personal data of another data subject, without their knowledge or consent, since Vodafone did not have a system in place to verify their identity.

The UK DPA (ICO) imposed a fine of around €12000 on HIV Scotland for failing to implement appropriate organisational and technical measures. The charity disclosed special category data by sending a group email in CC rather than BCC.

The Finnish DPA found that patients should be provided with a copy of their medical file free of charge under Article 15(3) GDPR, even when such a file includes X-rays and magnetic resonance images which cannot be printed on paper, but need to be burned on a CD/DVD.

The Polish DPA fined a controller approximately €80,000 for violating Articles 33(1) and 34(1) GDPR by failing to notify the DPA after a data breach, and only providing very general information regarding the breach to data subjects.

Three individuals complained that a cosmetics seller kept phoning them for product promotion, despite objections and, for some, registration in the Article 11 opt-out register. The company claimed oral consent and that the calls were customer satisfaction checks, but produced no proof of consent or of compliance with the legitimate-interest conditions. The Authority found breaches of Article 6, Article 21 and Article 12(2) GDPR. It imposed a single fine of EUR 20,000 for all breaches.

A patient complained that two pages of her psychiatric clinical diary, kept at a mental health centre of the Sardinia health agency, were mistakenly placed in another patient's copied records and handed to that person. The Garante found that health data was disclosed without a legal basis, breaching Articles 5 and 9 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 8,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were imposed because the conduct had ended and the agency had given assurances on organisational improvements. Mitigating circumstances included only two data subjects, a very short period, accidental human error during the Covid-19 emergency, full cooperation and prompt remedial action.

The Greek DPA decided that the Athens Bar Association (ABA) was allowed to share the personal data of its members with the candidates for the elections of the ABA, as long as the further processing of these data remains compliant with the GDPR.

The Luxembourg DPA found that a company was in breach of its obligation to communicate the contact details of its Data Protection Officer (DPO) under Article 37(7) GDPR, and of its obligation to ensure that its DPO does not have any conflict of interests under Article 38(6) GDPR.

The Danish DPA issued a warning against a company for breaching Articles 32(1) and 24(1) GDPR by failing to hide log files from its administrator accounts and to revoke administrator rights from an account it no longer used, both of which led to personal data about its employees being spread on the dark web.

The Spanish DPA fined Vodafone Spain €40,000 for violations of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR. The complainant received multiple invoices intended for a customer of the company and was not properly helped when they attempted to resolve this.

The CNPD ran a thematic audit campaign on data protection officers and opened an audit of a Luxembourg non-life insurance company in September 2018. The investigator alleged four failings. The restricted formation dropped the allegation on DPO qualifications because the company later showed the DPO had enough experience. It found breaches of Article 38.1 (DPO not properly involved in data protection matters) and Article 39.1.b (no adequate monitoring by the DPO at the start of the investigation). It imposed a single fine of EUR 13,200, lower than the EUR 23,400 proposed by the investigator, and declined some proposed corrective measures because the company had since taken steps.

Following an audit, the Luxembourg DPA (the CNPD) imposed a fine of €18,000 on a public entity because of four breaches relating to the role and position of its Data Protection Officer (DPO), and issued an injunction against that public entity to bring its practices in compliance with the GDPR.

The French DPA (CNIL) decided that the publication of its decision against the company 'Francetest' was justified given the sensitivity of the data processed and the need to ensure that all individuals concerned, as well as organisations using such services, are fully aware of the existence of persistent data security breaches.

The Austrian DPA held that a business-search platform's combination and cross-linking of public company register data about a director created new and value-added processing, but it was justified by the platform's and users' legitimate interests.

The Polish DPA (UODO) ordered a controller to provide a data subject with information on the marketing categories attributed to them on the basis of cookies, and to indicate which information concerning them was linked to the cookie information.

The Luxembourg DPA (CNPD) imposed a fine of €5300 on a company for using a video camera surveillance system on its premises and tracking devices in some of its employees' vehicles in breach of the information obligation set out in Article 13 GDPR and in breach of the principle of data minimisation set out in Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.
The Hellenic DPA fined a Greek company €1000 for violating Article 15 GDPR and Article 12(3) GDPR by not granting a data subject their right of access in due time.

A person who had entered ticket competitions on the controller's website monopoli.gr kept receiving newsletters despite repeatedly trying to unsubscribe and emailing the company. The unsubscribe function had been disabled during a CMS upgrade in December 2019, and the company did not manually remove the complainant even after being told. The Authority found that the right to object to direct marketing was not honoured and that the controller lacked an organisational measure to detect this, and imposed a EUR 5,000 fine under Articles 21(3) and 25(1) GDPR.

The Icelandic DPA ruled that a credit scoring company had violated the GDPR by assigning a credit score to an individual on the basis of information that was more than 4 years old. The Icelandic DPA therefore ordered the controller to delete the personal data in question.

The Icelandic DPA dismissed a complaint from two data subjects regarding the alleged recording of their house and backyard by the video cameras of their neighbors, after the latter demonstrated that the vision field of these cameras were restricted to their own private property.

The Icelandic DPA considered that, when an individual reports a case to the Children Protection Committee (CPC), the disclosure of that individual's name by the CPC to her employer, and further processing of her personal data by the employer, are contrary to the GDPR.

The Icelandic DPA ruled that the disclosure, by a law firm, of an individual's sensitive personal data is unlawful when the law firm fails to demonstrate that such a disclosure was necessary for the defence of its client's legal claim under Article 9(2)(f) GDPR.

The Austrian DPA rejected a complaint by two data subjects who claimed their right to confidentiality had been violated, and found the controller had lawfully obtained and processed the complainants' address data in the context of an advertising campaign.
The Spanish DPA (AEPD) fined a company €5,000 for transferring the data of an employee without the employee's consent.

The Norwegian DPA fined a road toll company about €499,373 (NOK 5,000,000) for not having a data processing agreement, risk assessment and transfer mechanism in place for transferring about 12,5 million car plate numbers to China, breaching Articles 5, 24, 32 and 44 GDPR.

The Icelandic DPA ruled that disclosing by mistake the email addresses of recipients of a bulk email was contrary to the GDPR. Given however that the controller took corrective measures to prevent such incident from happening again, no fine was imposed.
The French DPA held that a database containing over 6,000,000 fingerprints belonging to suspected or convicted offenders was mismanaged by the Ministry of the Interior.

The Hungarian DPA issued a reprimand against a controller for the unlawful recording and sharing of a private conversation between two parents and a daycare employee which contained special categories of data.
The Danish DPA (Datatilsynet) expressed serious criticism of the Danish Customs and Tax Administration's insufficient response to an Article 34(1) GDPR personal data breach.

The Danish DPA held that an online dating service had not obtained valid consent for its processing of personal data because it asked users to agree to its terms and conditions and privacy policy in the same tick box.

The Danish DPA recommended that a company involved in rapid COVID-19 testing of children aged 12 or over should provide processing information through booklets or pamphlets directly aimed at children.

The Norwegian DPA fined Ultra-Technology AS €12,785 (NOK 125,000) for conducting an unlawful credit rating, breaching Article 6(1) GDPR, and required the company to implement a policy for conducting credit ratings per Article 24 GDPR.

The Greek DPA found that a nursing home had unlawfully recorded its employees in violation of the principle of data minimisation and of the right to information. The Greek DPA instructed the nursing home to adjust the visual fields of some cameras and to destroy the already recorded material.

The Greek DPA held that sending bulk emails with all recipients' email addresses entered in the "To" field is not compliant with Article 32 of the GDPR. It recommended the use of BCC as an alternative.

The Icelandic DPA rejected a complaint from a data subject about the sharing of information between their previous, current, and potential future employers (i.e. public authorities X, Y and Z), which they argued led to an unlawful dismissal and rejection from new jobs.

A health clinic employee in Høylandet municipality, while creating letter templates, gained access to image files containing health data of real people with no connection to the municipality, held in the CGM patient system. The municipality reported the incident itself but took no adequate measures for about 11 months beyond asking staff not to open the files. Datatilsynet found a breach of Article 32 in conjunction with Article 24 GDPR, due to fundamental shortcomings in routines for shielding health data and handling deviations. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 400,000 and requested a report on the new routines.

St. Olavs hospital reported three deviations where patient information was stored in shared folders and files accessible to all authenticated users in the Central Norway health region, without access control or logging. The deviations lasted from about two to nine years and included about 21,000 cardiac reports, pulse oximeter reports and plaintext database passwords for substance abuse and child psychiatry clinics. The Norwegian DPA found breaches of security and internal control requirements (Articles 32, 24 and 5) and the Patient Records Act. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 750,000, noting the hospital's corrective measures and self-reporting.
The UK DPA fined a household repair company approximately €23,250 (GBP 20,000) for making 1,718 unsolicited direct marketing calls.

The Finnish DPA found that the Finnish police had unlawfully relied on the facial recognition software Clearview AI in 2020. It ordered the Finnish Police to bring processing into compliance with the GDPR and to notify identifiable data subjects of this breach.

A property owner complained that an associate of a real estate agency, La Prima S.r.l., contacted her on LinkedIn to offer real estate services for her property, having identified her as the owner from the land registry. The Garante found that using the registry data and the social network for promotion was incompatible with their purposes and had no legal basis (Arts 5, 6, 24, 25 GDPR). For these GDPR violations it issued only a reprimand and an order to adopt measures against promotion without a legal basis, because the case was isolated, the harm minor and the company a micro-enterprise. It imposed a EUR 5,000 fine for a separate violation, namely failing to answer the Garante's repeated information requests (Art. 157 of the Italian Code). A note says the later appeal ended in a final judgment of the Tribunal of Milan described as favourable.

A guest of an institute for the blind in Catania complained that video cameras had been installed in corridors and that visually impaired residents were not informed. The Garante found that, between 10 February and 19 October 2020, cameras filmed the corridor that three visually impaired residents had to use to reach the showers, which breached data minimisation. It also found the privacy notice was missing until June 2020 and afterwards incomplete and not suited to vulnerable people, and that no data protection impact assessment was carried out. The Garante fined the institute EUR 5,000, ordered it to provide the notice also in audio format, and ordered publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA fined the Commercial University of Milan €200,000 for violating Articles 5(1)(a), (c), (e), 6, 9, 13, 25, 35, 44 and 46 GDPR by using non-compliant supervisory systems as part of its provision of remote exams to students during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Italian DPA fined Sky Italia €3,000,000 for making unsolicited direct marketing calls, both independently and through call centres. It obtained the data necessary to make these through third party companies, thus unlawfully circumventing the requirement for data subjects to have consented to their personal data being used for promotional purposes.

A complainant reported that the municipality of Montalbano Jonico kept online, in the historical section of its official notice board, a payment determination naming the complainant and his disabled father, including health-related information, birth data, residence, address and details of works and invoices for removing architectural barriers. The municipality said this was a mere error between offices and that it had since redacted the data. The Garante found unlawful dissemination of health data, a breach of data minimisation, and publication beyond the 15-day period without a legal basis. It fined the municipality EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website. No further corrective measures were needed because the conduct had ceased.

The French DPA fined the Société Nouvelle de l'Annuaire Français, an online phone book company, €3,000 for infringing the right to rectification, the right to erasure and the obligation to have a record of processing activities.

The Belgian DPA closed a case after a data subject withdrew their complaint, because it considered that any potential infringements were inextricably linked to the willingness of the complainant to exercise their right to erasure pursuant to Article 17 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA fined Vodafone €56,000 for failing to authenticate a data subject, thereby allowing a fraudulent contracting for multiple new telephone lines. In this regard, Vodafone processed personal data without a legal basis according to Article 6(1) GDPR.
